content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.thinking:
I'm starting with a redesign of KasirKu's landing page—a POS and accounting platform built for Indonesian F&B, retail, and tourism businesses. The current site has that generic Tailwind template feel with green accents and rounded cards, but the user wants something with more visual punch. I need to build out a compact token system first that actually reflects what KasirKu does, then move away from the safe, templated aesthetic toward something more distinctive.

The key insight is grounding the design in what makes a cash register product special: receipts, the physical till, numerals, the tactile experience of Indonesian small commerce. A thermal receipt—with its perforated edges, monospace digits, and running tape of transactions—is a perfect visual metaphor that's both on-brand and completely different from generic SaaS templates. I can build the landing page around this receipt aesthetic instead of the typical centered hero with gradient backgrounds.

For the design system, I'm establishing a color palette that echoes receipt paper and the cash register experience: a warm off-white with a subtle green undertone as the base, paired with bold accent colors like jade or emerald green and a warm rupiah-orange or ink-black for contrast. The typography will use a dot-matrix or stencil display face for headlines to evoke that receipt printer feel, with a clean humanist sans for body text.

Now I'm refining the specific color tokens to avoid the typical AI-cliché cream tones. I'm leaning into thermal paper's actual appearance—which has a cool white or faint blue-grey cast—and incorporating hints of the brand green subtly. I'm defining the paper base as a pale sage-white, the ink color as a near-black with green undertones to suggest thermal print, and the accent as a bold saturated green for brand actions.

For secondary emphasis, I'm considering a warm stamp color—a deep vermillion red used sparingly and exclusively for rotated stamp effects like a "PAID" or "LUNAS" mark. Since my base isn't cream, pairing this warm red with the pale green-paper avoids the flagged cliché entirely while still giving the receipt design authentic character.

I'm also setting a dashed perforation line color as a light grey-green to reinforce the ticket aesthetic. For typography, I need something that evokes dot-matrix or receipt printer lettering—a bold condensed sans-serif would work well for headlines, evoking old cash register or market signage. The challenge is embedding fonts as data URIs since external CDNs are blocked by CSP, which means I need to work within the constraints of what I can actually self-host inline.

Rather than struggle with binary font embedding, I'll use a robust system font stack for the monospace ledger text—something like ui-monospace or Roboto Mono—which gives me the technical feel without needing to embed custom webfonts. This approach lets me achieve distinctiveness through scale, spacing, color, and layout instead. For the body text, I'll stick with a sans-serif stack that matches KasirKu's existing Arial usage, though since this is a marketing mockup rather than a live codebase update, I have flexibility to be more editorial with my choices. For the monospace elements in the ledger, I'm reaching for a system monospace stack.

The real typographic move here is making every number on the page render in tabular monospace—prices, stats, receipt line items—all styled like an actual receipt or ledger. That contrast between warm humanist sans for prose and rigid mono for numerals becomes the distinctive treatment, achieved entirely through native font stacks without risky custom font embedding. It's an honest design choice that leans into the tool's constraints and makes the sans/mono interplay plus the receipt-tape structure carry the visual identity.

For the layout, I'm envisioning a narrow centered column mimicking receipt paper width, with perforated dashed-line dividers between sections and headers styled like receipt headers—centered caps, tiny mono meta text like timestamps. The feature list becomes itemized line items with right-aligned values in monospace, and the CTA button gets styled like a rubber stamp (rotated slightly, stamp-red, saying "Mulai Gratis").

I'm reconsidering whether the entire page should be constrained to receipt-tape width—that could feel cramped and monotonous for a modern marketing page that needs to showcase dashboard screenshots and feature grids. Instead, I'll use the receipt motif as a strong visual frame: perforated edges at the top and bottom of the page like a torn receipt, dashed section dividers, mono numerals throughout, and the stamp-style CTA—while letting the layout breathe wide for grids and screenshots. That keeps the distinctiveness without sacrificing usability.

For dark mode, thermal receipts don't have a real-world dark analog, but I need to support it per the requirements.  I'll make a deliberate design choice: light mode represents a fresh receipt with pale paper and dark ink, while dark mode becomes a neon till display—like an LED cash register readout with a near-black background and phosphor-green or amber glowing numerals, warm off-white text. That creates a coherent inversion between paper receipt and LED display, both plausible cash-register artifacts.

Now I'm setting up the token plan with specific color values for both light and dark modes. Continuing with the typography system — display fonts use bold weight with tight tracking in mixed case to keep hierarchy flexible, while body text relies on regular weight with generous line-height for readability, and monospace is reserved strictly for all numerals, prices, and ledger-style metadata.

The whole landing page concept frames itself as a cash-register receipt — a full-bleed perforated card where the hero section mimics a receipt masthead with live-updating sales data instead of a static dashboard, sections are divided by dashed tear-lines, features are itemized like receipt line items with descriptions and right-aligned tags, the pricing section becomes the "TOTAL" line with a stamped CTA, and the footer echoes a receipt's bottom with a thank-you message, decorative barcode strip, and cut-line.

Now I'm grounding the content in KasirKu's actual offerings — the core features (F&B/Retail/Tempat Wisata, instant receipts, automated inventory and recipes, QR self-ordering, real-time reporting, payroll and attendance, customer data, multi-store security) plus the two new products that need prominence (HPP Calculator and Accounting System), all paired with the pricing tiers from the plans (monthly at Rp99.000, yearly at Rp990.000, lifetime at Rp2.500.000). The hero itself will be styled as a receipt with "KASIRKU" as the store name header.

I'm building an animated receipt display that cycles through live sales line items with a running total and a "LUNAS" stamp — this serves as both a product demo and the visual thesis moment. The animation will be straightforward, using a simple interval-based reveal for each line item with CSS transitions, and I'll respect the prefers-reduced-motion setting so it's accessible.

Now I'm checking my design choices against common defaults to make sure I'm not falling into predictable patterns — my palette is actually light paper with green-grey tones and terracotta used sparingly as an accent, the typography deliberately mixes system sans with mono for contrast rather than relying on a trendy web font, and the layout uses receipt-style perforated dividers instead of dense columns.

For icons, I'm ditching the emoji entirely since they clash with the receipt aesthetic — instead I'll use simple monochrome SVG glyphs or bracket-tag notation like "[F&B]" to keep that ledger-system feel. The layout won't be uniformly centered either; while the hero can lean center-aligned since receipts naturally do that, I'll vary alignment elsewhere to add visual interest. I'll build this as a standalone HTML mockup in an Artifact so the user can review the receipt-style redesign before I integrate it into the actual Next.js codebase. I'm planning the page structure with a perforated top edge, store header, and the rest of the sections following the ledger-style layout we discussed.

The header will feature the KASIRKU wordmark with address subtext, navigation links for the calculator and accounting system, and login/signup buttons styled with minimal ink-on-paper aesthetics. Below that, the hero section will showcase a live-cycling mock receipt as the centerpiece with primary and secondary CTAs. I'm organizing the "Untuk siapa" section as a business-type ledger with three rows for different business types, each with descriptive details, and then a feature list styled like receipt line items.

Cross-selling the other products as add-on items with pricing tags, followed by a pricing section that mirrors a receipt's total area with three plans displayed as ledger rows. The footer will replicate the bottom of a receipt with a decorative barcode strip, thank you message, and legal links. For the interactive hero, I'm planning an auto-typing effect that appends line items to create a sense of movement and life.

I'll use setInterval to loop through the items array, respecting prefers-reduced-motion by falling back to a static final receipt state. For number formatting, I'm applying `.toLocaleString('id-ID')` to handle Rupiah currency properly across any computed totals in the animation. Now I'm moving into the code itself, starting with a jade green as the primary color to give it a more distinctive visual identity while keeping it recognizably KasirKu.

Writing the HTML/CSS/JS file... I'm refining the headline to be punchier and receipt-themed while keeping the core value proposition intact—something like "Tiap transaksi, tercatat rapi — otomatis" that grounds the messaging in the receipt metaphor without losing the actual benefit of automated tracking and consolidated operations.

Now I'm structuring the hero section with a category eyebrow for F&B, retail, and tourism, a strong H1 about the cashier handling everything automatically, and a supporting subheading that walks through the full journey from point-of-sale transactions to monthly profit reports. I'm also mocking up a live receipt display cycling through realistic transaction items with prices and subtotals to make the automation tangible.

Finishing the receipt mock with tax calculation and a paid stamp, then laying out the business type descriptions, all eight core features, cross-sell products like the HPP calculator and accounting system with their pricing, and the standard pricing tiers ranging from monthly to lifetime options. The footer will repeat navigation links along with legal pages and copyright.

Sudah siap — ini **konsep rancangan visual baru**, belum diterapkan ke kode asli, murni buat kamu lihat dulu dan kasih masukan:

🧾 **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ac007e7b-481d-4888-be1b-cddd517b65e7**

Arah desainnya: seluruh halaman dibangun mengikuti tema **struk kasir sungguhan** — bukan template SaaS generik yang biasa dipakai di mana-mana. Beberapa hal yang saya sengaja beda dari desain lama:

- **Hero-nya bukan screenshot dashboard**, tapi struk yang "ngeprint" hidup — item demo muncul satu-satu, subtotal-PPN-total ke-update otomatis, lalu di-stempel "LUNAS". Ini sekaligus jadi demo produk beneran.
- **Semua angka pakai font monospace** (gaya kasir/ledger) — kontras dengan teks biasa yang pakai font standar. Ini yang bikin halaman berasa "kasir", bukan cuma warna hijau doang.
- Pembatas antar bagian pakai **garis putus-putus & tepi sobekan kertas**, bukan kartu bulat dengan shadow seperti kebanyakan situs SaaS.
- Tombol utama berbentuk **stempel tinta**, bukan tombol hijau polos.
- Fitur ditampilkan sebagai **daftar item struk** (nama — tag kecil di kanan), bukan grid kartu ikon emoji.
- Footer punya **barcode dekoratif + "TERIMA KASIH"**, khas struk asli.
- Sudah termasuk 2 produk baru (Kalkulator HPP, Sistem Akuntansi) sebagai "item tambahan", dan 3 paket harga asli (Rp99rb/Rp990rb/Rp2,5jt).
- Mendukung mode gelap dengan tema berbeda — versi gelap terasa seperti **layar LED mesin kasir** (angka menyala hijau phosphor), bukan sekadar warna dibalik.

content.thinking:
The user is giving feedback about the home page — they want to see more than just the dashboard view, with the ability to swipe through different page mockups.

They also checked on mobile and found that the product navigation links (Kalkulator HPP, Sistem Akuntansi, Artikel, Rekomendasi Alat) aren't visible in the header on mobile devices, only appearing in the footer, which makes them hard for customers to find. They want these links positioned higher up, near the login/signup section.

I'm realizing this feedback is probably about the actual live site rather than the new mockup I just showed them, since they mention checking on their phone and don't reference any of the new design elements. This aligns with the recent changes I made where I hid those nav links on mobile using `hidden md:block` styling — exactly what they're complaining about. The user's first point is about the hero section on the live site — they want the static Dashboard card transformed into a carousel that cycles through multiple app screens (Dashboard, POS/Kasir, Laporan, etc.) so users can swipe left to see what else the app offers. The second point about mobile nav links being hidden is the real usability issue I created with the responsive classes.

I went too far hiding all navigation links on mobile, which defeats the purpose of improving discoverability. The "Produk kami" section (Kalkulator HPP, Sistem Akuntansi) and other nav links need to stay accessible on mobile, not disappear until the footer. Since the landing page doesn't have a mobile menu system like the dashboard does, I should add a hamburger menu button that toggles a dropdown listing all the key links — that's the quickest way to surface everything without cluttering the mobile header.

I'll need to create a client component for the interactive toggle since the page is likely a server component, then position the hamburger button next to the Masuk/Daftar Gratis buttons so it's discoverable exactly where the user feedback indicated it should be.

For the hero carousel, I'm thinking of building a swipeable component that cycles through different dashboard views (Dashboard, POS/Kasir, Laporan, etc.) with touch gesture support for mobile and dot indicators to show which slide is active. The "geser kiri" feedback makes it clear users expect swipe functionality.

Let me check the current state of src/app/page.tsx to see what I'm working with for the header and hero section.

Continuation of [[product-roadmap-2026-07]] item #3 ("redesain tampilan website... lebih nendang"). Two separate threads happened the same day — keep them distinct:

**1. Concept mockup, not yet applied to real code**: built a full alternate-direction landing page as a standalone Artifact (not touching the live Next.js site) themed entirely around a **cash-register receipt** — thermal-paper palette (pale green-grey, not the AI-cliché warm cream), tabular monospace for every number, dashed perforation dividers instead of rounded cards, an ink-stamp-style primary CTA, and a live-animating "printing receipt" hero (line items appear one by one, totals update, ends with a LUNAS stamp) instead of a static dashboard screenshot. Dark mode reimagined as an LED cash-register display (phosphor-green digits on near-black) rather than a naive color inversion. Covers real KasirKu content (all 8 features, 3 business types, the 3 real pricing tiers, cross-sell to Kalkulator HPP Desktop and Sistem Akuntansi) — no lorem ipsum. **Status: shown to user for feedback, not yet approved or ported into the actual codebase.** If resumed, check whether the user reacted to this direction before starting from scratch on a new one — the artifact URL was `https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ac007e7b-481d-4888-be1b-cddd517b65e7` (private, machine/session-specific, may not resolve in a future context — ask the user if it's still relevant).

**2. Live-site mobile UX fixes — DONE and shipped 2026-07-16** (`05eecad`), reported by the user after checking the actual production site on their phone (separate from the mockup above, on the real `src/app/page.tsx`):
- **Hero preview was static** (only ever showed the "Dashboard" stat card + bar chart). New `src/app/hero-preview.tsx` (client component) turns it into a 3-slide carousel (Dashboard / Kasir / Laporan — each a distinct realistic mini-mockup of that part of the app) that auto-advances every 3.2s (respecting `prefers-reduced-motion`), supports touch swipe (`onTouchStart`/`onTouchEnd` delta-X threshold 40px), and has clickable dot indicators. Implemented as a CSS-transform sliding track (`translateX(-active*100%)`), not a library.
- **Product/content nav links were invisible on mobile entirely** — a regression from the earlier same-day commit `f3eb589` that bumped Kalkulator HPP/Sistem Akuntansi to `sm:` and Artikel/Rekomendasi Alat to `md:` breakpoints to reduce header crowding, which had the side effect of hiding all 4 on phone-width screens (only reachable by scrolling all the way to the footer). Fixed with new `src/app/home-mobile-nav.tsx` (client component, `sm:hidden`) — a hamburger button positioned in the header immediately before Masuk/Daftar Gratis (per the user's explicit ask, "sebelah Masuk-Daftar Gratis") that toggles a dropdown with all 4 links.
- **Tooling note**: the hamburger button's first `computer`/click-tool click didn't register (`aria-expanded` stayed `"false"`) — same class of plain-onClick-button flakiness already documented in [[test-account-preview]] for the POS PIN pad. Switched to `javascript_tool` `.click()`, which worked, though even then the `aria-expanded` read immediately after the same script's `.click()` call showed stale `"false"` (React state update hadn't flushed yet) — had to read it in a *separate* subsequent `javascript_exec` call to see `"true"`. If a toggle button's state looks unchanged right after a scripted click on this project again, don't assume the click failed — re-query in a follow-up call before concluding it didn't work.

content.thinking:
The callback flow looks right—the code exchange sets the session cookie, then redirects to `/reset-password` with that session now active. But there's a wrinkle: `/reset-password` is marked as public in the middleware, yet at this point the user would actually be authenticated, which creates a logic conflict I need to think through.

Actually, I think I've found the issue—if `exchangeCodeForSession` fails (returns an error), the callback route redirects straight to `/login`, which matches exactly what the user is experiencing. The code exchange itself might be failing, possibly because the email link isn't actually sending a proper PKCE code parameter from Supabase.

Looking at the middleware comment, it hints at this: the reset password link from email arrives as a URL fragment token (`#access_token=...`), not as a query string `code` parameter. So when the callback route checks `if (code)`, it finds nothing and falls through to the login redirect. The token needs to be handled client-side by the Supabase JS library instead. it redirects to `/login` instead. The middleware comment actually reveals the real design intent — `/reset-password` should receive the recovery link directly without going through `/auth/callback`, letting the Supabase client automatically detect the fragment token in the URL and establish a session client-side, which then allows the password update to succeed.

The fix is straightforward: change the `redirectTo` in the forgot-password form from pointing to `/auth/callback?next=/reset-password` to just `/reset-password` directly, so the recovery link lands on the right page with the token fragment intact and the session gets established immediately. But this raises a question — the middleware comment describes this fragment-based approach as the intended design from an earlier implementation, yet the current forgot-password code doesn't follow that pattern at all.

This mismatch could mean either the auth flow was originally built to use `/reset-password` directly but got changed at some point (breaking it in the process), or the project's Supabase settings actually use a newer PKCE recovery flow with a code parameter instead of a hash fragment, in which case the real issue might be something like a mismatched code verifier in cookies — a common PKCE problem when the initial recovery request and the final code exchange happen in different browser sessions or devices.

But actually, this reasoning points back to the first explanation: Supabase specifically uses hash-fragment tokens for password recovery emails precisely because those links get opened in a fresh browser context (often a different device) where the original PKCE code verifier wouldn't exist. So recovery emails from Supabase are virtually always hash-based regardless of project PKCE settings, which means routing through `/auth/callback` (which expects a `code` parameter) would almost always fail for password recovery, causing exactly the behavior the user is seeing.

The real fix is to have the forgot-password flow redirect directly to `/reset-password` instead of `/auth/callback`, letting the Supabase client automatically detect and process the hash fragment when that page loads. Since the browser client has `detectSessionInUrl: true` by default, it should handle the session setup automatically without needing special waiting logic.

input.content:
---
name: auth-forgot-password-fix
description: "Forgot-password flow bug fixed 2026-07-16 — was silently falling back to /login instead of the reset-password form"
metadata:
  type: project
---

User reported: "pada saat lupa password kembali seperti dulu mengarah ke login, bukan ubah password" — clicking the password-reset link from email landed on `/login` instead of the "buat password baru" form.

**Root cause**: `src/app/forgot-password/page.tsx`'s `resetPasswordForEmail` call had `redirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/reset-password`. `/auth/callback` (`src/app/auth/callback/route.ts`) only knows how to exchange a `?code=` query-string param for a session (PKCE flow) — but Supabase password-recovery emails always carry the token as a URL **fragment** (`#access_token=...&type=recovery`), never as `?code=`, specifically because the recovery link is opened in a browser/device that never held the original PKCE code verifier (email links get opened anywhere, not necessarily the same browser that requested the reset). Since fragments never reach the server, `/auth/callback` always saw `code=null` and fell through to its `redirect(/login)` fallback — 100% of the time, not intermittently.

Ironically, `src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts` already had a comment explaining this exact fragment-token mechanic as the reason `/reset-password` is a public path — the intended design was clearly for the email link to land directly on `/reset-password` so `supabase-js`'s browser client (which auto-processes URL fragments on load via `detectSessionInUrl`) could establish the session client-side. `forgot-password/page.tsx` just wasn't actually pointing there.

**Fix** (`dee0010`): changed `redirectTo` to `${origin}/reset-password` directly, bypassing `/auth/callback` entirely for this flow. `/auth/callback` is still correct/needed for other code-exchange flows (email confirmation etc.) — this was specifically about the recovery-link redirect target.

Verified: form submission succeeds against the Dev Supabase project (see [[supabase-dev-prod-split]]) and shows the "Cek email kamu" success state; `/reset-password` loads directly without a middleware redirect even fully unauthenticated (confirming the public-path allowlist works). Could not verify the full click-the-real-email-link path end-to-end (no email inbox access in this environment) — if this regresses again, that's the step to check manually.

**Tooling note**: the first submit-button click via the `computer` tool silently no-op'd (no network request fired) — same class of hydration-race flakiness already documented in [[test-account-preview]] for other forms on this project. A second click, then finally a `javascript_tool` `.click()` call, worked. Don't assume a form is broken from one failed click.

**How to apply**: if any future auth-related redirect flow (email confirmation, magic link, invite) needs a `redirectTo`, check whether Supabase issues that particular email type with a `?code=` (safe to route through `/auth/callback`) or a `#access_token=...` fragment (must redirect straight to the page that will consume it client-side) — don't assume every auth email link is code-exchange-compatible.

I'm debugging an "Auth session missing" error report in a Next.js + Supabase app at G:\PROJECT1\KasirKu. The user said (in Indonesian): "belum ada 1 menit saya ketik pasword baru dan lama sudah auth session missing" — roughly "within less than a minute of typing new and old password, [I got] auth session missing".

I already know about and just fixed `src/app/reset-password/page.tsx` (the public password-recovery flow reached via a "lupa password" email link) — that page only has "Password Baru" and "Ulangi Password" fields, NO "old/current password" field, since it's a recovery-token-based flow.

The user's mention of typing "password baru DAN LAMA" (new AND old password) suggests they might be somewhere else — possibly a "change password while logged in" feature in account/business settings that asks for current password + new password, which would be a completely different code path with its own possible causes for "Auth session missing".

Please search this codebase (particularly under src/app/business/*/settings/, src/app/dashboard/, src/app/account/, or anywhere else plausible) for:
1. Any page/component that has BOTH a "current/old password" field AND a "new password" field in the same form (search for Indonesian terms like "Password Lama", "Password Saat Ini", "Ganti Password", "Ubah Password", as well as English "current password", "old password").
2. Any call to `supabase.auth.updateUser` or `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword` or similar auth methods outside of src/app/reset-password/page.tsx and src/app/forgot-password/page.tsx.
3. Report back: does such a "change password" feature exist elsewhere in this app? If yes, give me the exact file path(s), and show me the full relevant component code (especially the submit handler) so I can diagnose why it might throw "Auth session missing". If no such feature exists anywhere else in the codebase, say so clearly and list what password-related pages DO exist (just reset-password and forgot-password?).

Also check: does `src/lib/supabase/client.ts` or any auth config have anything unusual about session persistence, cookie domain, or session timeout that could cause a freshly-established session to disappear within under a minute?

This is research only — I will do the actual fix myself. Report back concisely with file paths and relevant code, under 400 words if possible.

content.text:
## Findings

**No "change password while logged in" feature exists anywhere in the codebase.** I searched all of `src/` for Indonesian terms ("Password Lama", "Password Saat Ini", "Ganti Password", "Ubah Password") and English ("current password", "old password", "currentPassword", "oldPassword") — zero matches. I also grepped every `supabase.auth.*` call site: only `src/app/reset-password/page.tsx` (`updateUser`) and `src/app/login/page.tsx` (`signInWithPassword`) touch auth directly.

**Password-related pages that DO exist**, all confirmed by reading their code:
- `src/app/login/page.tsx` — email + password, `signInWithPassword`
- `src/app/signup/page.tsx` — registration (has "password" per grep, not read in full but no old-password field per the broader search)
- `src/app/forgot-password/page.tsx` — sends recovery email
- `src/app/reset-password/page.tsx` — the one you already fixed; only "Password Baru" + "Ulangi Password" (`updateUser({ password })`), no old-password field, confirmed above
- `src/app/business/[businessId]/(dashboard)/cashiers/reset-pin-form.tsx` — a cashier PIN reset (not account password)
- `add-cashier-form.tsx` and `void-ticket-transaction-form.tsx` — incidental "password" text hits, unrelated to account password change

The `settings/` directory under `business/[businessId]/(dashboard)/` is business config (tax, printers, payment methods, ticket categories) — no account/password form there. No `src/app/account/` or `src/app/**/profile/` directory exists at all.

**Conclusion:** the user's "password baru dan lama" ("new and old") almost certainly just refers colloquially to typing the new password twice in the confirm field on `reset-password/page.tsx` (or possibly confusion/mistranslation), not a separate settings flow — since no such flow exists in this app.

**Session config** (`src/lib/supabase/client.ts`): plain `createBrowserClient` from `@supabase/ssr`, no custom `auth` options (no `persistSession`, `autoRefreshToken`, storage, or cookie-domain overrides) — defaults apply, nothing unusual there.

**Middleware** (`src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts`): has a detailed comment explaining `/reset-password` is deliberately excluded from the auth-gate because the recovery link's `access_token` arrives in the URL fragment and is only readable client-side by supabase-js — "belum ada sesi/cookie sama sekali saat request pertama ini sampai ke middleware." That's the most likely root cause area for the "Auth session missing" report (fragment-based token race/timing before the client establishes the session), consistent with what you already fixed.

The "Auth session missing" error from `supabase.auth.updateUser()` is a specific Supabase error that fires when there's no active session at all, which means the session derived from the reset link's hash fragment never got established or was lost by the time they submitted the form. Given they managed to reach and interact with the reset-password page in under a minute, the most likely culprit is that an email security scanner (like Outlook's Safe Links or a corporate mail gateway) pre-fetched and consumed the reset link before the user actually clicked it.

Other possibilities: `detectSessionInUrl` might not be processing the hash correctly in the `@supabase/ssr` browser client, or there's a mismatch in the Supabase Auth redirect URLs allowlist. The actual flow is that Supabase's hosted `/auth/v1/verify` endpoint validates the OTP token server-side, then redirects to our app's redirect URL with the session tokens appended as a hash fragment—this explains why the session should be available in the URL when the page loads.

Given this design, the "Auth session missing" error after landing on `/reset-password` almost certainly means either our client-side code never processed the hash, or the token was already consumed before the user's browser loaded the page—like if an email scanner or preview service hit the verify endpoint first, exhausting the single-use token, so by the time the real user arrives, Supabase's verify endpoint either redirects without valid tokens or includes an error parameter instead of the access token.

The most robust fix from our side is to explicitly check for an active session on the reset-password page mount using `supabase.auth.getSession()` or listening for the `PASSWORD_RECOVERY` auth state event, and immediately show a clear Indonesian message like "link sudah tidak valid/kedaluwarsa, minta link baru" if no session exists—rather than letting users fill out the form only to hit a cryptic error at submit time. The issue likely stems from the `code_verifier` requirement in PKCE — when `exchangeCodeForSession(code)` is called, it needs the matching `code_verifier` that was generated and stored when `resetPasswordForEmail` was initially called, and this only works reliably when the same browser/session completes the flow, which becomes problematic for password recovery scenarios where users might click the link on a different device or after clearing cookies. So the real issue is that Supabase generates the recovery link with `?code=` parameters specifically because the client is configured for PKCE flow, not hash-based tokens — and GoTrueClient's initialization should detect and auto-exchange this code, but something in that detection or exchange is failing, which is why the user sees "Auth session missing" even though the code is present in the URL. handles both `code=` parameters for PKCE and hash fragments for implicit flow automatically, validating that the detected flow type matches what the client was initialized with. But wait — the code_verifier cookie needs to be present in the browser when the user lands on `/reset-password?code=...` for the exchange to succeed. If that cookie was cleared, lost between sessions, or never set properly when `resetPasswordForEmail` was called, the auth exchange will fail with "Auth session missing" because there's no way to complete the PKCE flow without it.

The real issue is that PKCE recovery flows are inherently fragile when the recovery link opens in a different context — this is a well-known problem, which is why Supabase specifically recommends using an implicit flow for recovery instead of relying on the shared client's PKCE configuration. The robust fix would be to explicitly switch to implicit flow for the recovery process, since recovery emails need to work regardless of whether the user's browser state has been cleared. ach for password recovery — the email template needs to include the token hash in the confirmation URL, and then the reset-password page verifies it directly with `verifyOtp()` using that token hash and recovery type, which exchanges it for a session without needing the PKCE code_verifier. Since I can't control the dashboard template from app code alone, and the immediate priority is fixing the bug reliably with code changes, I'm weighing the most practical option: setting `flowType: 'implicit'` explicitly on the browser client to override the SSR package's default PKCE behavior.

A second click, then finally a `javascript_tool` `.click()` call, worked. Don't assume a form is broken from one failed click.

**How to apply**: if any future auth-related redirect flow (email confirmation, magic link, invite) needs a `redirectTo`, check whether Supabase issues that particular email type with a `?code=` (safe to route through `/auth/callback`) or a `#access_token=...` fragment (must redirect straight to the page that will consume it client-side) — don't assume every auth email link is code-exchange-compatible.

---
name: auth-forgot-password-fix
description: "Forgot-password flow — two-round fix 2026-07-16, final root cause was @supabase/ssr's hardcoded PKCE flowType breaking cross-device recovery links"
metadata:
  type: project
---

Two bugs, found and fixed in sequence the same day — the first fix was real but incomplete; keep both rounds in the record since the second round's root cause supersedes the first's explanation.

**Round 1**: user reported clicking the password-reset email link landed on `/login` instead of the "buat password baru" form. Or this could be a dark mode issue—if the user's system is in dark mode and there's a global CSS rule that lightens text color for dark mode, but the input background is hardcoded to white, the text would become nearly invisible light-on-light. I found the issue—when dark mode is enabled, the CSS variables are being set correctly, but the `--foreground` color is being applied as the text color on the body, which makes the text nearly white on what should be a dark background.

The problem is that form inputs aren't explicitly overriding this inherited text color, so they're displaying near-white text (#ededed) on their default white backgrounds, making the text nearly invisible. This matches exactly what was reported—the input text is hard to read or sometimes not visible at all. The bug wasn't caught earlier because there's no explicit grey Tailwind class on the inputs themselves; the issue comes from the inherited color property cascading down from the body's dark mode styles. The safest fix is to remove the `prefers-color-scheme: dark` media query entirely since this codebase doesn't have a real dark mode design — everything else uses explicit light Tailwind classes. I should search the codebase to confirm that the `background` and `foreground` custom color utilities aren't used elsewhere before removing them.

content.thinking:
The TTFB metrics show a cold start of 1.6 seconds and warmed-up requests around 0.65-0.67 seconds, which is reasonable for a Vercel serverless function handling SSR with Supabase authentication checks. The homepage is calling `getUser()` on every request to determine if visitors should be redirected to the dashboard, and that auth check involves a network call to Supabase.

For anonymous visitors (the majority of homepage traffic), this auth check is unnecessary latency on the critical path. I'm considering whether to skip the server-side auth check entirely for the marketing homepage and instead handle the redirect via client-side logic or middleware, since the redirect-if-logged-in behavior is a convenience rather than a security requirement. Let me verify whether the middleware already handles this case — it marks "/" as a public path, so I need to check if the middleware's user-checking logic would catch logged-in users before they even reach the homepage component.

Actually, I'm realizing the real issue: the middleware already calls `getUser()` during session updates on every request, and then the homepage's Server Component independently calls `getUser()` again — that's a redundant duplicate auth check hitting Supabase twice for the same request. Since middleware runs first at the edge layer, the homepage shouldn't need its own separate auth call; it could rely on the session data that middleware already refreshed.

Fixing this across the entire app would require passing user data from middleware through request headers to Server Components, which is doable but a significant refactor with broad blast radius. For now, I should focus on the isolated case of the homepage's redundant `getUser()` call and see if removing that specific call improves performance without requiring a full architectural change.

The measured TTFB of 0.65–1.6 seconds is moderate and likely within normal range for Vercel's free tier plus a Supabase round trip, especially depending on network location. I should report this baseline and flag the double `getUser()` pattern as a plausible inefficiency, while acknowledging I don't have real user profiling data to confirm it's the dominant bottleneck.

Before diving into a large refactor across the whole app, I'll apply the CSS dark-mode fix I've already prepared, commit it, then come back with a concrete performance report and a clarifying question about whether "lemot" refers to slow initial page loads or sluggish interactions after the page is loaded—those have very different root causes and solutions.

The middleware's `updateSession()` call is doing legitimate session refresh work for cookie management, so I need to figure out which calls are truly redundant versus necessary.

The key insight is that middleware already fetches the user for session refresh purposes, so I could pass that information down to the page via request headers instead of making a second call just to decide whether to redirect logged-in users to the dashboard.

This requires modifying middleware to inject the user data into headers, then updating every Server Component that currently calls `getUser()` independently to read from those headers instead. The scope of changes depends on how many files are actually making auth calls — the earlier search suggested it's fairly limited, but I should verify that before committing to this approach.

The user's complaint about slow first-load likely refers to the homepage specifically, so I could start by optimizing just that page as a lower-risk proof of concept that directly addresses the TTFB issue they mentioned.

I'm considering swapping `getUser()` for `getSession()` on the homepage — it would skip the network round-trip to Supabase's Auth API and just decode the JWT locally from cookies instead. The tradeoff is that `getSession()` doesn't re-validate the token server-side, so Supabase warns against using it for authorization decisions, though for initial page load it might be acceptable. This is a straightforward, low-risk optimization: switching the homepage's auth check from `getUser()` to `getSession()` eliminates an unnecessary network call by just reading the JWT cookie locally, which is safe here since we're only deciding whether to show a redirect prompt, not actually protecting content. Three issues reported together in one message; two fixed, one still open.

**1. Kembalian (change due) low contrast — FIXED** (`af06d94`): the change-due amount shared the same muted `text-zinc-500`/`text-zinc-600` as its label everywhere it's shown (POS payment panel in both `pos-screen.tsx` and `ticket-pos-screen.tsx`, plus the transaction/ticket detail pages) — bolded + darkened the value (`font-bold text-zinc-900`) in all 4 spots, left the label muted. Not verified live in browser (needs either a real cashier PIN session or seeded transaction data with `change > 0`, neither readily available in the fresh Dev Supabase project — see [[supabase-dev-prod-split]]) — only `tsc`/`eslint` clean. If this ever needs re-checking, that's the gap.

**2. Form text nearly invisible in dark mode — FIXED** (`bd39dc6`): root cause was `src/app/globals.css`'s leftover default-Next.js-template `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` block, which flipped `body`'s `color` to `#ededed` (near-white) whenever a visitor's OS was in dark mode. Every component in this app uses explicit light-mode Tailwind classes (`bg-white`, `text-zinc-900`, etc.) — nothing else in the codebase actually reads `--background`/`--foreground` (confirmed via grep, zero other matches) — so this was a genuinely half-implemented, unused dark-mode remnant. Any element that doesn't set its own explicit text color (the login/signup email/password inputs, specifically) inherited that near-white body color and rendered on a white input background — nearly invisible, exactly matching the report ("kadang ga keliatan sama sekali"). Removed the dark-mode block entirely rather than patch around it, since there's no real dark-mode design to preserve. Verified in browser: forced dark `prefers-color-scheme` via `resize_window`'s `colorScheme` param, confirmed `getComputedStyle` on the email input showed `color: rgb(23,23,23)` (dark, readable) instead of the old near-white — fix holds regardless of visitor OS theme.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing a timing discrepancy — Neraca is showing a balance sheet as of July 16, 2026, but the journal entry is dated July 17. Since the system clock has passed midnight in WIB timezone, the entry from 00:04 on the 17th falls after the cutoff time of the previous day, so it's being correctly excluded from the report. The question is whether this behavior is actually a bug or working as intended.

Looking at how Neraca calculates its default date, if it's using UTC-based date computation instead of WIB, that would explain the issue — at 00:04 WIB on the 17th, UTC is still showing the 16th, so the default "as of" date would be yesterday relative to local time. This would create a real timezone bug where for the first 7 hours of each WIB day, today's entries are silently hidden from the balance sheet. Let me test this by explicitly passing the date parameter to see if July 17 entries appear.

content.thinking:
I'm identifying the UTC-based date bug across five different pages in the application—each one defaults to today's date using UTC instead of the local WIB timezone, causing incorrect dates to display between midnight and 7 AM. The affected areas span accounting reports, journal entries, cash tracking, invoices, and finance pages.

I also notice that the receivables, purchases, and ticket reports have the same issue, plus several member-related pages that compare against today for expiry checks. The export route and one fallback in the reconciliation file are affected too. Some modules like payroll and the dashboard already handle WIB correctly, but reconciliation is inconsistent—it uses UTC in one place and WIB in another.

The solution is to create a shared helper function that returns today's date in WIB format and apply it consistently across all these buggy locations instead of letting each file handle the timezone conversion separately.
Saya menemukan 11 titik yang masih menggunakan UTC daripada WIB, terutama bermasalah di jam 00:00–07:00 WIB. Sekarang saya akan membuat helper bersama dan memperbaiki semuanya.

---
name: ui-bugfixes-2026-07-16
description: "Two small UI bugs fixed 2026-07-16 (Kembalian contrast, invisible dark-mode form text) plus an open performance investigation"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: a6d0af07-7540-4516-bd00-24ac48a5c53b
---

Three issues reported together in one message; two fixed, one still open.

**1. Kembalian (change due) low contrast — FIXED** (`af06d94`): the change-due amount shared the same muted `text-zinc-500`/`text-zinc-600` as its label everywhere it's shown (POS payment panel in both `pos-screen.tsx` and `ticket-pos-screen.tsx`, plus the transaction/ticket detail pages) — bolded + darkened the value (`font-bold text-zinc-900`) in all 4 spots, left the label muted. Not verified live in browser (needs either a real cashier PIN session or seeded transaction data with `change > 0`, neither readily available in the fresh Dev Supabase project — see [[supabase-dev-prod-split]]) — only `tsc`/`eslint` clean. If this ever needs re-checking, that's the gap.

**2. Form text nearly invisible in dark mode — FIXED** (`bd39dc6`): root cause was `src/app/globals.css`'s leftover default-Next.js-template `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` block, which flipped `body`'s `color` to `#ededed` (near-white) whenever a visitor's OS was in dark mode. Every component in this app uses explicit light-mode Tailwind classes (`bg-white`, `text-zinc-900`, etc.) — nothing else in the codebase actually reads `--background`/`--foreground` (confirmed via grep, zero other matches) — so this was a genuinely half-implemented, unused dark-mode remnant. Any element that doesn't set its own explicit text color (the login/signup email/password inputs, specifically) inherited that near-white body color and rendered on a white input background — nearly invisible, exactly matching the report ("kadang ga keliatan sama sekali"). Removed the dark-mode block entirely rather than patch around it, since there's no real dark-mode design to preserve. Verified in browser: forced dark `prefers-color-scheme` via `resize_window`'s `colorScheme` param, confirmed `getComputedStyle` on the email input showed `color: rgb(23,23,23)` (dark, readable) instead of the old near-white — fix holds regardless of visitor OS theme.

**3. General "lemot"/slow feeling on the live site — PARTIALLY ADDRESSED** (`414cf01`): user confirmed this is specifically about slow **initial page load** (not post-load interaction lag) on the deployed production site. Measured via `curl -w`: homepage TTFB ~0.65s warm, ~1.6s cold before the fix — not catastrophic but not fast.

**Root cause found and fixed for the homepage specifically**: `src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts`'s `updateSession()` already calls `supabase.auth.getUser()` on every request (necessary — refreshes the session per Supabase's documented Next.js pattern), and `src/app/page.tsx`'s `Home` Server Component was **independently calling `getUser()` again** — a second Auth-API round-trip on the critical path of every single homepage load, purely to decide whether to redirect an already-logged-in visitor to `/dashboard`. Swapped to `getSession()` (reads the already-refreshed cookie locally, no network call) since this specific check is a UX nicety, not a real access-control boundary.

**Deliberately left alone** (audited via `grep supabase.auth.getUser` — 7 total call sites): `middleware.ts` itself (must stay `getUser()`, that's the one that actually refreshes the cookie), `business/[businessId]/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` (real subscription/access gate), `dashboard/page.tsx` and `admin/page.tsx` (list/show real per-user data), `onboarding/actions.ts` and `billing/actions.ts` (mutations tied to a specific authenticated user, e.g. payments) — all of these need the server-validated `getUser()`, swapping them to `getSession()` would weaken real security checks, not just an optimization.

**Not yet done / open**: this only speeds up the homepage's own redundant check — it does NOT address whatever the dashboard, POS, or other pages' first-load latency looks like (each has its own render path and hasn't been profiled). Also unexplored: Vercel cold-start latency, Supabase query latency inside the dashboard/business pages (some report pages do multiple sequential queries), and client-side bundle size. **How to apply**: if "lemot" persists after this homepage fix, next ask specifically *which* page(s) still feel slow to open (dashboard? POS? a report page?) and profile that page's own request waterfall rather than assuming the same getUser()-duplication pattern is the cause everywhere — it was confirmed only for the homepage.

Pemeriksaan menyeluruh selesai. **Hasilnya: semua fitur utama berfungsi, dan saya menemukan + memperbaiki 1 bug baru yang cukup serius.**

## Yang diperiksa & hasilnya

**Pemeriksaan otomatis** — semuanya lolos: 41/41 unit test, typecheck bersih, lint bersih di seluruh kode.

**Uji alur lengkap di browser** (pakai database dev, akun test baru dari nol):
- ✅ Login → onboarding buat toko → gate langganan (halaman billing muncul dengan 5 paket termasuk Finance Only) → aktivasi → dashboard terbuka
- ✅ Tambah produk, tambah kasir + PIN, buka POS, mulai shift, checkout tunai — **Kembalian tampil tebal & gelap** (fix kemarin terkonfirmasi)
- ✅ **Cetak struk langsung buka dialog print otomatis** (fix kemarin, yang sempat tertahan belum ter-commit, sekarang sudah ter-commit & terverifikasi — dialog print-nya yang "membekukan" halaman justru bukti fiturnya jalan)
- ✅ Penjualan otomatis masuk Jurnal dengan double-entry seimbang (Kas 15rb/Pendapatan 15rb + HPP 6rb/Persediaan 6rb), angkanya konsisten di Laba Rugi, Kas Harian, dan Laporan
- ✅ Semua halaman Akuntansi, SDM, Operasional, dan halaman publik (landing, sistem-akuntansi, kalkulator-hpp, blog, dll) — 200 OK semua, nol error console

## Bug baru yang ketemu & sudah diperbaiki (`d662a6c`)

**"Hari ini" dihitung pakai jam UTC, bukan WIB, di 13 halaman.** Gejalanya nyata: transaksi yang saya buat jam 00:04 WIB **tidak muncul di Neraca** karena Neraca masih menganggap "hari ini" = kemarin. Setiap hari antara jam 00:00–07:00 pagi, halaman Neraca, Rekonsiliasi, dan semua form tanggal (jurnal, kas harian, invoice, pembelian, piutang, pengeluaran) serta cek masa berlaku member akan salah satu hari. Sudah diperbaiki dengan satu helper terpusat dan diverifikasi langsung — Neraca kini menampilkan tanggal & angka yang benar.

Semua sudah di-push, Vercel akan deploy otomatis. Kondisi aplikasi sekarang: siap dipakai, tinggal urusan launch prep yang sudah kita catat (harga final Finance Only + menunggu approval Midtrans).

10	Built 2026-07-12, closing the #1 launch blocker identified in a full codebase audit (see [[project-purpose-saas-product]]): before this, there was no way for anyone to pay for KasirKu at all. User's decisions that shaped the design: both a recurring subscription AND a one-time lifetime purchase (not subscription-only), **Midtrans** as the gateway, **no trial** (must pick+pay immediately after signup), and a **3-day grace period** (past_due banner) before a lapsed subscription actually locks the account out.
11	
12	**Schema** (migrations `20260712110000_billing.sql` + `20260712120000_admin_billing_columns.sql`): `public.subscriptions` (one row per business, mutated in place — `status` unpaid/active/past_due/expired, `plan_code`, `period_end` null=lifetime) and `public.payments` (append-only Midtrans transaction log). RLS is deliberately narrow: a business can SELECT its own rows and INSERT exactly one `unpaid` subscription (at onboarding) / any number of `pending` payments (to start a Midtrans transaction) — but can never write `active`/`settlement`/etc itself. Only the service-role Midtrans webhook and cron sweep can transition status, so a tenant can never mark itself paid. Plan catalog (name/price/period) is a **TS constant** (`src/lib/billing/plans.ts`), not DB-driven — fast to ship, revisit if pricing needs to change without a deploy. **Prices are placeholders** (Rp99rb/bulan, Rp990rb/tahun, Rp2,5jt lifetime) — must be edited before real launch, no real pricing input was given.
13	
14	**Existing businesses were grandfathered** — the billing migration backfills every pre-existing business with a permanent `active`/`lifetime`/`period_end=null` subscription row, so toko-toko test yang sudah ada tidak mendadak terkunci begitu migrasi jalan. This was almost missed — caught before applying the migration, not after.
15	
16	**Enforcement**: two independent Server Component layouts do the actual lockout — `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` and a new `pos/layout.tsx` — both call `getSubscriptionAccess()` (`src/lib/billing/status.ts`) and `redirect()` to `/business/<id>/billing` if locked (`unpaid`/`expired`). Deliberately NOT one shared `[businessId]/layout.tsx` wrapping everything, since that would redirect-loop on the billing page itself (Next.js layouts can't easily detect "am I currently the billing page"). `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` also shows a past_due warning banner (amber, in `dashboard-shell.tsx`) with a link to `/billing` — pos doesn't need the banner, cashiers don't need to see billing state.
17	
18	**Payment flow**: `billing/actions.ts` `createPayment()` inserts a `pending` payment row, then calls Midtrans Snap's create-transaction API (sandbox vs production host picked via `MIDTRANS_IS_PRODUCTION`), returns a `redirect_url` the client does a plain `window.location.href` to (no Snap.js popup SDK). Webhook at `src/app/api/midtrans/notification/route.ts` verifies the `sha512(order_id+status_code+gross_amount+MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY)` signature, uses a **new service-role Supabase client** (`src/lib/supabase/service.ts` — first use of `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in this codebase, only ever import this in the webhook/cron, never in user-facing code), flips `payments.status` and (idempotently — checks for already-`settlement` first) activates the subscription, extending `period_end` from the greater of now-or-existing-period_end (so early renewal doesn't lose paid days). Daily cron (`vercel.json` + `src/app/api/cron/subscription-sweep/route.ts`, guarded by `CRON_SECRET` bearer header) ages `active`→`past_due` (period_end passed) →`expired` (past_due + 3 days).
19	
20	**Bug found and fixed during E2E testing**: `src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts`'s public-path allowlist didn't exempt `/api/*` routes, so Midtrans's webhook and Vercel's cron caller — both server-to-server with zero browser session — were being redirected to `/login` instead of reaching the route handler at all. Fixed by adding `/api/midtrans` and `/api/cron` to `isPublicPath`. Caught by literally curling the webhook locally and getting back the string `/login` instead of JSON — a good reminder to always hit new API routes with a bare curl (no cookies) as part of verifying them, not just through the browser (which carries a session and would have masked this).
21	
22	**Verified E2E 2026-07-12, all without needing real Midtrans credentials** (used a locally-set dummy `MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY`/`CRON_SECRET` in `.env.local` just to exercise the signature/auth logic, plus a Node script using the real `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` to backdate `period_end` directly via the REST API since RLS blocks the owner from writing to `subscriptions` themselves):
23	- Existing "Toko Test Laporan" stayed fully accessible after the migration (grandfather confirmed).
24	- Fresh signup → onboarding → landed on `/billing` (not `/dashboard`), status "Belum Berlangganan"; direct URL access to both the dashboard and `/pos` correctly redirected back to `/billing`.
25	- Clicked "Bayar Sekarang" (lifetime plan) → pending payment row created, Midtrans rejected the fake key with a real API error surfaced cleanly in the UI (confirms the actual HTTP call shape is correct, just needs real Sandbox keys next).
26	- Hand-crafted a correctly-signed `settlement` webhook payload (order_id pulled via a REST call using the browser's own session cookie, signature computed with Node's `crypto`) → `payments.status` → `settlement`, `subscriptions.status` → `active`, `plan_code` → `lifetime`, `period_end` → `null`. Dashboard unlocked immediately after.
27	- Cron sweep: backdated an `active` monthly subscription's `period_end` to yesterday → sweep flipped it to `past_due` (dashboard still reachable, amber banner present, confirmed via `document.body.innerText.includes(...)` since the banner sits outside `<main>` and `get_page_text` only grabs `<main>`). Backdated further to 4 days past → sweep flipped to `expired` → dashboard redirected to `/billing` again, showing "Kedaluwarsa".
28	- Security: webhook with a wrong `signature_key` → 401. Cron with no/wrong `Authorization` header → 403.
29	
30	**Still needed before this can go actually live** (not done, no real credentials available this session): real Midtrans Sandbox `MIDTRANS_SERVER_KEY`/`MIDTRANS_CLIENT_KEY` in `.env.local` to test the real Snap-hosted checkout redirect; the same billing env vars set in Vercel's environment settings for deploy; the webhook URL (`https://<domain>/api/midtrans/notification`) registered in the Midtrans dashboard's payment notification settings; then swap to production keys + `MIDTRANS_IS_PRODUCTION=true` when ready. Also no admin UI yet to manually comp/override a tenant's billing status (e.g. for an offline bank-transfer edge case) — flagged as a fast-follow, not built.
31	
32	**Update 2026-07-12, same day**: user registered a real Midtrans business account ("Createimpact.id", perorangan) via the newer unified "MAP" onboarding at passport.midtrans.com — business verification came back "Dalam proses, aktif dalam 2-3 hari kerja" (not instant). Tried the account's Access Key page (`dashboard.midtrans.com/settings/access-keys`) keys anyway against our Sandbox API host — Midtrans rejected with "Access denied due to unauthorized transaction, please check client or server key", confirming this newer onboarding flow does NOT give you working Sandbox-testable keys immediately; both sandbox and production calls are gated behind the same verification. User chose to skip waiting on it for now rather than try the old separate `dashboard.sandbox.midtrans.com` classic-sandbox route.
33	- **Interim solution built**: `src/lib/billing/config.ts` — `BILLING_MANUAL_MODE` (currently `true`) + `BILLING_CONTACT` (WhatsApp `6281234556757`, email `create2impact.id@gmail.com`). When true, `billing/page.tsx` renders WhatsApp/email contact links (pre-filled with plan name + business name via `wa.me`/`mailto:` query params) per plan card instead of the `PayButton`/Midtrans flow, so customers still have a way to pay manually while the Midtrans account clears review. The actual Midtrans integration code is untouched — this is purely a display-layer toggle in the billing page. **Flip `BILLING_MANUAL_MODE` back to `false` once Midtrans keys are confirmed working** (retry the same Sandbox-key test once the account's 2-3 business day review completes).
34	
35	**Manual admin activation — built 2026-07-12, same day**: since manual/WhatsApp-coordinated payment has no automated confirmation, added `admin_activate_subscription(p_business_id, p_plan_code, p_period_days, p_amount, p_note)` (migration `20260712130000_admin_activate_subscription.sql`) — security-definer, checks `private.is_admin()`, mirrors the webhook's exact period-extension math (`greatest(now(), coalesce(existing period_end, now())) + period_days`), records a `payment_type='manual'` row in `payments` for the same audit trail. New `"Tandai Sudah Bayar"` control per business row in `/admin` (`src/app/admin/activate-subscription-form.tsx` + `src/app/admin/actions.ts`) — click to expand a plan-picker + optional note, confirm to activate. **Not yet E2E-verified in browser**: attempting to temporarily grant the test account admin access (an insert into `public.admins` via the service-role key) was blocked twice by the auto-mode permission classifier as an unapproved privilege-escalation write, even after the user said yes in chat — the classifier wants the grant named more explicitly/directly than a follow-up "ya boleh" could satisfy. Fell back to asking the user to test it themselves with their real admin account instead. If asked to verify this again, don't retry the self-grant approach — ask the user to test directly, or ask them to explicitly pre-authorize the specific grant before attempting it.
36	
37	**Two production bugs found this same day, both fixed and deployed**:
38	1. Midtrans's new account onboarding ("MAP", passport.midtrans.com) put the user's account in "Dalam proses, aktif 2-3 hari kerja" — tried the Access Key page's keys against our Sandbox API host anyway, got "Access denied due to unauthorized transaction, please check client or server key". Confirms this onboarding flow gates both sandbox and production behind the same review, unlike the classic separate `dashboard.sandbox.midtrans.com` instant-sandbox route (user chose not to try that route, went with `BILLING_MANUAL_MODE` instead).
39	2. **Real production bug, unrelated to billing**: `/reset-password` was never added to `src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts`'s `isPublicPath` allowlist. A password-reset email link carries its recovery token in the URL hash fragment, which only `supabase-js` running client-side can read — the server-rendered middleware sees an unauthenticated request to a non-public path and redirects to `/login` before the page (and its token-processing JS) ever loads, silently breaking every password reset attempt in production. Fixed by adding `/reset-password` to the allowlist (same class of bug as the earlier `/api/midtrans`/`/api/cron` fix — see above). Caught because the user's own real account (m.khamdannn91@gmail.com) needed a password reset to test the admin panel and it kept failing. Deployed via commit `494726d`.
40	
41	**Postgres gotcha hit while migrating**: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` fails with `42P13 cannot change return type of existing function` when you add new OUT-parameter columns to a `RETURNS TABLE(...)` function (here, extending `admin_list_businesses()` with `subscription_status`/`plan_code`). Fix is `DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS ... ; CREATE FUNCTION ...` instead of `CREATE OR REPLACE` — worth remembering for any future RPC signature change, see [[supabase-migrations-manual]].
42	
43	**Midtrans onboarding update 2026-07-14**: account activation moved past "Business review" (step 3/4, see [[kalkulator-hpp-desktop]]) — Midtrans emailed asking for one more document before activation: a PDF "Flow Transaksi" showing the customer journey from browsing to checkout/payment page (with payment methods shown), submitted via a one-off `sales-tooling.midtrans.com/merchant-form/...` upload link (not the main dashboard). Built `private-assets/flow-transaksi-createimpact.pdf` (reportlab-generated diagram, not literal screenshots — user chose "describe + placeholder" over toggling `BILLING_MANUAL_MODE` for real screenshots) covering both flows sharing this one merchant account: KasirKu subscription (`/business/{id}/billing`) and Kalkulator HPP Desktop one-time purchase (`/kalkulator-hpp/beli`), both ending at a described Midtrans Snap hosted payment page. **User still needs to actually upload this PDF to the sales-tooling form themselves** (Claude does not submit third-party business forms) — check back next session on whether it was accepted and whether real Access Keys have arrived.
44

content.text:
Berikut panduannya — singkat saja karena prosesnya memang sederhana:

**1. Pilih tempat beli (registrar) — untuk Indonesia yang umum:**
- **Niagahoster** / **Domainesia** / **Rumahweb** — lokal, bayar bisa via transfer/e-wallet/QRIS, support Bahasa Indonesia
- **Cloudflare Registrar** atau **Namecheap** — internasional, sedikit lebih murah, bayar pakai kartu

**2. Cek nama yang tersedia.** Di situs registrar ada kolom pencarian domain. Coba variasi: `kasirku.com` (kemungkinan sudah diambil), `kasirku.id`, `kasirku.co.id`, `pakaikasirku.com`, dll. Perkiraan harga per tahun:
- `.com` → sekitar Rp150-250rb
- `.id` → sekitar Rp250-300rb (kesan lokal & kredibel untuk pasar Indonesia)
- `.co.id` → mirip `.id` tapi **butuh dokumen legalitas usaha** (NIB/SIUP), lebih ribet
- `.my.id` → murah banget (Rp10-30rb) tapi kesannya kurang profesional untuk produk berbayar

Saran saya untuk KasirKu: **`.id` atau `.com`**, mana yang tersedia dengan nama bagus.

**3. Saat checkout — yang penting:**
- ✅ Cukup beli **domainnya saja**
- ❌ **Tolak semua tawaran hosting/email/SSL** — kamu tidak butuh, situsmu sudah di-hosting Vercel dan SSL-nya otomatis gratis dari Vercel
- ✅ Kalau ditawari "WHOIS privacy / proteksi privasi" gratis, ambil (menyembunyikan data pribadimu dari publik)

**4. Bayar → domain jadi milikmu** (per tahun, jangan lupa perpanjang).

**5. Setelah beli, kasih tahu saya nama domainnya.** Saya pandu langkah menyambungkannya ke Vercel — cuma 2 langkah: tambah domain di dashboard Vercel, lalu isi 1-2 record DNS di dashboard registrar. Sekitar 10-15 menit termasuk nunggu propagasi, dan situs langsung jalan di domain baru (yang `kasirku-nine.vercel.app` tetap hidup sebagai cadangan).
